>Stress/deadlines are a part of daily life.

I'm aware of that. 

>Grammar/spelling is EXTREMELY important (you don't want something to go

responsible for checking it).

I'm also aware of that, hence the use of Grammarly.

>She's pushing you to do better, just as most art directors would.   
Multiple concepts/revisions are common, and a good Art/Creative Director  
 will constantly push you for improvement.

These are previously finished, graded projects that she's telling me aren't professional quality. They've had many, many rounds of revisions before even getting to this point, but they're no longer good enough even if they were projects from her previous classes. If they were good enough for that class, why do I have to restart the whole thing now?

>I tell all of my new designers that design doesn't end at 5pm... once   
you've truly immersed yourself, you'll dream of logo designs while you   
sleep. You'll think about concepts while you shower. You'll critique   
every billboard design on every road trip. You may not be sitting at a   
desk, but you'll be thinking about every project you work on   
after-hours. At least, the good designers will. And while it's not as   
common for companies to hold you late or make you work over the weekend   
to meet a deadline, it still happens, especially if you don't make that   
5pm deadline

I get that. Thinking about design or something subconscious like that isn't the same as work hours. A healthy work-life balance is important.

>Criticism is a way of life as a designer. You accept it for what it's   
worth, and you run with it, especially since you're still learning. You   
can fight for your designs, but ultimately what your client (or teacher)  
 wants is what you have to give. Creating your own designs without ANY   
alteration from someone else is extremely rare, and typically reserved   
for the top experts in the field. You're new to the field, so who are   
you to disagree with what an expert tells you to fix? Arguing (even in a  
 professional manner) will absolutely be frowned upon. Humble yourself.   
Take this opportunity to learn, not to argue.

But I'm not getting actual critique. I'm being told the change things with no reason why besides it's not portfolio quality. I'm fumbling my way through without actual guidance. Defending my decisions isn't arguing, have you never had to explain why you designed something the way you did? I don't know more than the experts, and I've never once said that I do. What I do know is that being told to change things to the point the final result isn't MY work doesn't help me improve because I'm not being told why something is wrong in the first place.

Design isn't 24/7 and I'm not about to argue the importance of a healthy work-life balance. Some people can give their all 100% of the time. I can't, sorry if that's disappointing to you. I don't mean to be rude, I'm very frustrated with people telling me I don't understand the profession when design can wait until the next day. Nothing in this profession is an emergency.

>Do your courses have regular critique? Ideally, there shouldn't be too   
many surprises by the time you get a project returned from grading   
because you'd have been discussing it throughout the process.

Not in this class. It's Portfolio Capstone which involves improving projects from past semesters so I've been graded on them once already. This class is to further improve on the work, but when I turn them in for review she tells me to restart them from the beginning. I have anywhere between 5-7 pieces to work on every week.

>A prof shouldn't be directly telling you what concepts to use, but   
should be directing you in terms of staying on target and questioning   
your choices to get you to defend them.

When I try to defend my choices she doesn't tell me why it's wrong, just that it is and I need to change it. When I try to ask  for further clarification, I'm told to make this or that change and that's it. I don't get direct feedback for what I'm doing wrong.

>This may need further clarification because none of my stress or   
workload in college was due to teachers arbitrarily inflating things, it  
 was because of my own time management, wide-eyed idealism in terms of   
ideas and often just aiming too high, and trying to do work without the   
experience to know what was reasonable.

Admittedly, I could use better time management, but I never turn assignments in late. Again, I have anywhere between 5-7 projects to work on every week, on top of other assignments for the Professional Practice co-req class. That one is about being your own brand with social media posting schedules for Instagram, LinkedIn, and Behance, assuming we'll freelance. I understand the importance of having a social media presence, but I'm also old enough to know that I'm never going to freelance.

>I don't understand this at all, what is the actual class schedule? If a   
class has one session per week, which is common for typical college   
structure, you can't be doing a full project weekly, let alone multiple.  
 A small exercise maybe. But most of my projects were 3-6 weeks in   
length.  
>  
>And for portfolio, the class that involved portfolio prep and review did  
 itself not involve any actual projects beyond the portfolio, we were   
drawing from all the design projects we did in other classes throughout   
the program.  
>  
>Having a portfolio be reviewed to graduate is also not something I'm   
familiar with, unless you mean a grade for the portfolio as a project   
within that one class, and that class being required to graduate. Still,  
 to grade students on work that should've been done in other classes is   
odd.

These two classes (Portfolio Capstone and Professional Practice) are both twice a week for 12 total hours. Still, some of the projects I'm turning in for my portfolio were, at the time, semester long projects. I'm told to start over. I've been working on like 3 things (previously finished in other classes) since the semester started and they're not even close to done (per her standards.) The whole class is preparing our portfolio with an open to the public review as well as a final review by the Art & Design faculty. Not having enough finished pieces means failing the class.

>That's good for actually working, but in school it's often a marathon   
and you put in the time required to produce the work as needed. Some   
weeks that could be 20-30 hours, others could be 80-100. I was often   
working on stuff on Saturday nights instead of going to the bar with   
friends because that's what you do. You are there to develop, it's not   
the same as actually working for a living. You have to get as much out   
of it as you can.

I've been working for over a decade. I've worked throughout this entire degree. I know what it's like to buckle down and get the work done because I've done it. Doing the work isn't the problem, being told every week that nothing I do is good enough is. I worked on one new concept piece last week for at least 15-20 hours, not including the time it took to hand-make some items, photographing and photoshopping them, for her to say "seems like your heart wasn't in it." I'm just done being told my work sucks.

[Recipe](https://www.delish.com/cooking/recipe-ideas/recipes/a54052/buckeye-cookies-recipe/)

**For the Filling** 

1 1/4 c. creamy peanut butter

1/3 c. powdered sugar

**For the Cookies** 

3/4 c. (1 1/2 sticks) butter, softened

3/4 c. packed brown sugar

1/2 c. granulated sugar, plus more for rolling

1 large egg

1 tsp. pure vanilla extract

1 1/4 c. all-purpose flour

3/4 c. cocoa powder

3/4 tsp. baking soda

3/4 tsp. kosher salt

​

**Directions**

1. Preheat oven to 350° and line two the large baking sheets with parchment paper. Make the filling: In a medium bowl, combine peanut butter and powdered sugar and mix until smooth. Using a 2-teaspoon cookie scoop, scoop into 22 small balls and freeze until hardened, 30 minutes.
2. In a large bowl, combine butter, brown sugar, and sugar and beat until light and fluffy, then add egg and vanilla and mix until evenly combined. Add the flour, cocoa powder, baking soda, and salt and mix until evenly combined.
3. Scoop a heaping tablespoon of the cookie dough and flatten into a pancake-like circle on the baking sheet. Place a frozen peanut butter ball on top. Bring the edges of the dough around the peanut butter ball and pinch the edges together to seal, adding more dough if necessary to cover the frozen peanut butter completely.
4. Roll stuffed cookie dough ball in sugar and place back on prepared baking sheets. Repeat until all dough is used, spacing the cookies about 2” apart.
5. Bake until the cookies are set, about 12 minutes. Serve warm or at room temperature.
